hops.afterHeading: The map: ranges, fibres and channels
hops.title: How rattlesnakes sense a mouse's warmth
hops.text: Rattlesnakes are often said to see infrared. The detector is not in their eyes, though, and it runs on no light-sensing chemistry. Infrared from a nearby animal warms a thin membrane stretched across a pit between each eye and nostril. In 2010, Elena Gracheva, David Julius and colleagues showed that the nerve fibres supplying that pit carry TRPA1, one of the channels in the table above. In lab recordings, western diamondback TRPA1 opened at about 27.6 °C. Versions from a boa and a python opened at about 29.6 and 32.7 °C. The snake is, in effect, feeling the mouse from across the sand.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A coiled rattlesnake on desert sand at dusk, head raised toward a small field mouse beside a cactus.
image.caption: Infrared from prey warms the pit membrane, which opens TRPA1 in the nerve fibres inside it.

hops.afterHeading: Three channels for one burn: redundancy, not a chain
hops.title: A boy who ate hot peppers without the burn
hops.text: Doctors examined one boy repeatedly from the age of three, because he ate large amounts of hot peppers with no aversion, no blotchy skin and no tears. When researchers studied him at eleven, he carried two copies of a mutation, N331K, that left his TRPV1 channel non-functional. Capsaicin on his mouth or skin did nothing. Heat still hurt, though. He detected gentle warmth as well as healthy volunteers did and still felt heat pain, at a higher threshold. Mustard oil, which opens TRPA1, gave him markedly more redness and irritation than the volunteers. Losing one channel erased the chili burn, not heat pain altogether.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A bright red chili pepper on a wooden cutting board with a small bowl of chili peppers behind it.
image.caption: With no working TRPV1, chili never burned this boy, though heat still hurt him above a higher threshold.

hops.afterHeading: A different question: where is the sensor inside the channel?
hops.title: Ground squirrels and camels with heat-dulled TRPV1
hops.text: Thirteen-lined ground squirrels and camels cope with high temperatures better than many other mammals, and in 2016 Laursen and colleagues found unusually weak heat responses in their TRPV1 channels. Capsaicin still opened both. A single amino acid swap in the channel's N-terminal ankyrin-repeat region restored strong heat responses to the squirrel and camel channels, and the reverse swap dulled heat sensitivity in rat TRPV1. Heat opening and chemical opening can therefore be pulled apart inside one protein. A residue that shifts the threshold still does not say whether that spot senses the heat or only passes it to the gate.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A striped ground squirrel standing upright beside its burrow in sunlit short grass.
image.caption: One amino acid swap restored strong heat responses to squirrel and camel TRPV1; capsaicin worked before and after.

audio.title: Three surprises from temperature channels
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories about temperature channels doing jobs nobody expected of them.

The first comes from the common vampire bat. It feeds only on blood and uses warm spots on an animal's skin to locate where blood runs close to the surface. For that it has three small pits, called leaf pits, arranged around its nose. In twenty eleven, Elena Gracheva, David Julius and their colleagues worked out how those pits sense heat. The bat did not invent a new receptor. The sensory neurons that serve its face splice the channel's R N A in a different way and make a shorter version of T R P V one, the painful-heat and chili channel from this lesson. The short form is sixty-two amino acids shorter at one end. In lab recordings it opened at about thirty degrees Celsius, compared with about forty for the long form. The R N A transcript for that short form makes up roughly a third to nearly half of the T R P V one transcripts in the ganglia serving the face, and less than three percent in the ganglia serving the body. The nose gets a sensitive warmth detector while the long form can still work as a heat alarm elsewhere.

The second story is in your own eyes. Even when nothing is bothering them, your eyes make a slow, steady supply of basal tears all day. In twenty ten, researchers in Spain showed that cool-sensitive nerve endings on the cornea, the clear front of the eye, help regulate that flow, and that they depend on T R P M eight. These endings track small swings in the temperature of the eye's surface and change their firing to match. Mice without T R P M eight lose the cornea's cold responses and make fewer basal tears, yet they still tear up normally when something actually irritates the eye. In people, gently warming the cornea lowers the tearing rate. Like the cool line in the mouse forepaw, a quiet cold sensor turns out to be doing a job you would never have filed under temperature.

The third story is about a drug. Once T R P V one was tied to heat and inflammatory pain, it looked like an obvious target for new painkillers, and researchers built a selective blocker called A M G five seventeen. In human trials reported in two thousand eight, the blocker caused marked hyperthermia, a rise in body temperature. In a molar extraction trial, body temperature rose in every participant who received the blocker. In about a third of them, it reached thirty-nine to forty point two degrees Celsius and stayed elevated for one to four days, and in one person it went past forty degrees Celsius. In rats, the same blocker narrowed the blood vessels in the skin of the tail and raised the body's own heat production, and either change can push body temperature up. The trials made the point plainly. T R P V one is not a simple pain switch that can be shut off without consequences. Blocking it acutely can push human body temperature up, tying a channel best known for sensing burns directly into temperature regulation.
